Muse Spark 1.1, the latest release in the Muse Spark family of models developed by Meta Superintelligence Labs.1 Muse Spark 1.1 builds upon Muse Spark 1.0, the model introduced in the Muse Spark Safety & Preparedness Report (Meta Superintelligence Labs et al., 2026).
[meta-muse-spark-1-1-system-card] Muse Spark 1.1 is the updated model powering Meta AI, succeeding Muse Spark 1.0 alongside new product features.
[meta-muse-spark-1-1-system-card] Moreover, Muse Spark 1.1 is also released to external developers through an application programming interface (API) that surfaces agentic affordances, including tool and function calling and user-specified developer prompts.

[meta-muse-spark-1-1-system-card] Agent Robustness (Section 3.2). The majority of threat models evaluated in this section assume an attacker can leverage user-connected third-party tools to execute multi-step malicious plans.
[meta-muse-spark-1-1-system-card] This assumption applies to the current deployment setting.
[meta-muse-spark-1-1-system-card] For direct tool misuse, we evaluate Muse Spark 1.1 on the verified subset of AgentHarm against our content safety policy.
[meta-muse-spark-1-1-system-card] Muse Spark 1.1 demonstrates strong robustness against misuse requests while maintaining a lower false refusal rate on the benign set relative to peer models such as GPT-5.5.
[meta-muse-spark-1-1-system-card] We continue to harden these surfaces through adversarial training and system-level safeguards such as an injection detector for oversight and action-level intervention.
[meta-muse-spark-1-1-system-card] 3.2.1 Robustness Against Direct Misuse 3.2.1.1 AgentHarm Verified We evaluate broader agentic misuse with AgentHarm (Andriushchenko et al., 2024), a public benchmark measuring whether tool-using agents complete explicitly malicious, multi-step tasks.
[meta-muse-spark-1-1-system-card] As an update for this release, we use AgentHarm Verified, a subset filtered through an AI-assisted human review that retains only prompts which are genuine violations of our content policy, removing non-violating cases from the open-source set.
[meta-muse-spark-1-1-system-card] This resulted in 108 verified disallowed behaviors.
[meta-muse-spark-1-1-system-card] To validate whether the model roll-outs contain violations, in addition to a standard refusal judge, we also include a policy-auditing LLM to check for false positives—cases where the model’s completion was not a direct violation but instead a safe redirection of the malicious user query.
[meta-muse-spark-1-1-system-card] There are two subsets in AgentHarm Verified: 50 a subset with malicious user requests and a subset of benign user requests.
[meta-muse-spark-1-1-system-card] We report the Average Harm Score (AHS) on the malicious set and the False Refusal Rate (FRR) on the benign subset.

[meta-muse-spark-1-1-system-card] We report the Average Harm Score (AHS) and the False Refusal Rate (FRR) for each model.
[meta-muse-spark-1-1-system-card] For model rollouts on this benchmark, we observed cases where the model flags the tools or task as potentially synthetic or fictional.
[meta-muse-spark-1-1-system-card] Across multiple Muse Spark 1.1 checkpoints, roughly 10% of chain-of-thought traces raise concerns that the scenario is a safety test or that the user request may not be genuine.
[meta-muse-spark-1-1-system-card] When AgentHarm’s tasks and tool constructions were first created, they served as useful proxies for measuring how resilient LLMs were to pursuing harmful goals—especially since models at that time were far less capable than current LLMs.
[meta-muse-spark-1-1-system-card] As we look ahead to evaluating adversarial robustness in future deployment contexts, we will include benchmarks that measure more complex agentic misuse.
